description: We’re Team NEXORA, a group of college students who are really into space. We wanted to make rocket science something you learn by actually doing it, not just by reading about it. Each of us took on a different part of the project, from design and programming to art, sound and the write up. Together we built Rocket Lab, a game where you build your own rocket, launch it and fly it all the way to the Moon, and pick up how real rockets work along the way.
summary:
Rocket Lab – Design It. Launch It. Reach the Moon. is a pixel-art game where players design, launch and fly their own lunar missions. They choose a payload based on their mission objectives, which include releasing a satellite in lunar orbit, deploying a rover, or landing a crew to build a return rocket. If they choose the rover deployment goal, they must drop a rover in a target zone on the lunar surface. Meanwhile, crewed mission challenges involve making a soft landing, building a return rocket while considering mass, thrust, fuel, and budget, and managing live readouts during construction.
The flight runs on real physics: gravity, air drag, thrust, staging and orbits. On the way up, players face hurdles drawn from real launches. They ease the throttle through Max-Q, hold steady in wind shear, free a jammed stage, dodge a rock field, push through a radiation belt and aim through the trans-lunar window. Choosing a later launch time pays more but brings stronger wind and more rocks. Satellites and rovers they deliver stay on, scouting landing sites that make later missions easier, so every choice carries forward.
New players can start in Flight School, where a expert guides them through building their first rocket and flying it to the Moon, explaining the science as they go. Failed flights show what went wrong, so players learn spaceflight by trying, failing and improving.
details:
Team NEXORA’s Project Solution

Rocket Lab – Design It. Launch It. Reach the Moon. is a pixel-art educational game about rocket engineering and lunar exploration. Players become mission designers: they build a rocket for a chosen payload, launch it, fly it through real spaceflight hazards and try to complete a mission at the Moon.

Every design decision affects the outcome. Players balance thrust against mass, choose fuels, manage a budget and steer through challenges such as Max-Q and a jammed stage separation. When a mission fails, the results show what went wrong, so players learn by improving their rocket and trying again.

How Does Our Solution Work?

The game takes players through the complete journey of a lunar mission, starting with rocket construction and ending with mission evaluation. Players must make engineering decisions at every stage, understand the consequences of their choices, and improve their designs to achieve successful missions.

1. Main Menu and Mission Selection

Players begin at the Rocket Lab main menu, where their rocket stands on the launch pad. The menu offers:

  • Continue: Pick up a saved game.
  • New Game: Start fresh with a new save.
  • Flight School: Learn how to play with guided lessons.
  • Options: Turn sound, the guide’s voice and fullscreen on or off.
  • Exit: Leave the game.

When players start, the rocket lifts off and the game moves into the Rocket Lab.

2. Need Lessons ? Visit Flight School

Flight School is the game’s learning section, where a Mission Control radio voice guides players step by step. It offers two guides:

  • Rocket Lab Guide: A tour of the rocket-building lab covering every part, the telemetry panel, the lift gauge, the bank and the mission card. Each stop has a Tell Me More card explaining the science, such as why a rocket’s thrust must be greater than its weight before it can lift off.
  • Game Guide: Players build a real rocket from a picture, one step at a time, then fly it all the way to the Moon. Mission Control pauses the flight at each new challenge to explain what to do. If the rocket crashes, the flight rewinds to the last checkpoint so players can try again.

3. Rocket Builder – Design Your Own Rocket

In the Rocket Lab, players first choose a payload, which decides their mission:

  • Crew: Carry astronauts to a soft landing on the Moon.
  • Satellite: Place a satellite in a stable orbit around the Moon.
  • Rover: Drop a rover into a target zone on the lunar surface.

Heavier payloads need bigger rockets. Players then build their rocket with these parts:

  • Nose Cone: Reduces air drag.
  • Structural Blocks: Form the main body of the rocket.
  • Fuel Tanks: Store the fuel for the journey.
  • Boosters: The engines that push the rocket upward.
  • RCS Thrusters: Small gas jets that steer the rocket in space, where fins don’t work.
  • Fins: Keep the rocket flying straight through the air.

A telemetry panel shows the rocket’s mass, thrust, fuel and lift as it is built. Every part adds capability, but also weight and cost, so the biggest rocket is not always the best one.

4. Fuel Selection and Budget Management

Each fuel has a real trade-off:

  • Kerosene: The starter fuel, cheap and dependable.
  • Hydrogen: Lighter and more efficient, so the rocket goes further, but it pushes less. It must be unlocked for $150.
  • Cold Gas: Used only by the RCS thrusters for steering.

Every part has a price, paid from the player’s bank, and successful missions earn money for better rockets. Players must balance performance against cost instead of simply building the largest rocket possible..

5. Launch Preparation and Launch Window

Before launching, the rocket must pass the game’s launch checks. The Launch button stays locked until the rocket has a payload, fuel and a booster, and the player can afford it. The Lift gauge turns red and shows Too Heavy if the thrust can’t beat the rocket’s weight. On the launch pad, a quick test flight predicts how far the rocket will get, such as “Reaches space: add fuel for the Moon”, so players can go back and improve the design first.

Players then choose a launch window:

  • Dawn: Calm wind and few rocks, standard reward.
  • Noon: More wind and rocks, 1.25× reward.
  • Dusk: Strong wind and many rocks, 1.5× reward.
  • Night: The hardest conditions, double reward.

This teaches players that a successful launch needs the right design and the right moment.

6. Flight Simulation and Spacecraft Control

Once the rocket launches, players fly it themselves. The flight follows real physics: gravity pulls the rocket down, air slows it, the engine pushes it up, and the rocket gets lighter as fuel burns. Players control:

  • Throttle (W / S): Increase or reduce engine power.
  • Steering (A / D): Tilt the rocket left or right.
  • Engine and Stages (X / B): X stops the engine. In space, B drops the empty side parts of the rocket to make it lighter, just as real rockets do.

Live panels show fuel, lift, direction, health, height and the current mission phase. Losing parts or taking damage lowers health, and if it reaches zero the mission fails.


7. Flight Challenges

On the way to the Moon, players face six challenges, most based on real rocket launches. The height bar on the right side of the screen shows where each one is coming up:

  • Max-Q: The air pushes hardest on the rocket here. Players lower the throttle so the rocket isn’t damaged.
  • Wind Shear: Strong winds push the rocket sideways. Players steer to keep it pointing up.
  • Jammed Stage: A part gets stuck when it should drop away. Players tap its key quickly to free it.
  • Rock Belt: Rocks fly toward the rocket. Players dodge them by steering and changing speed.
  • Radiation Belt: Radiation slowly damages the rocket and mixes up the readings on screen.
  • Trans-Lunar Window: Players aim the rocket so a needle lands in the green, putting it on course for the Moon.

    Getting through a challenge cleanly earns a reward. Failing one costs health or fuel, and can end the mission.

8. Lunar Orbit and Mission Execution

After the flight challenges, players reach the Moon. The rocket arrives too fast to stay, so players fire the engine to slow down until the orbit gauge’s Low and High points both turn green, meaning a stable lunar orbit. Each payload then has its own objective:

  • Satellite Mission: Hold the stable orbit and release the satellite.
  • Rover Mission: Drop the rover when its marker is over the green landing zone. There is only one chance.
  • Human Landing Mission: Drop out of orbit and land the crew softly on the landing site.

Players must watch their direction, speed and fuel throughout. Satellites and rovers stay on the Moon after the mission and scout landing spots, making future missions easier.

9. Mission Results and Performance Evaluation

After every flight, Mission Control radios the result, and the results screen shows:

  • Mission success or failure.
  • Performance score and stars.
  • Earnings and the new bank balance.
  • Mission goals completed.
  • Options to retry or return to the Rocket Builder.

Each failure points to something to improve, such as too little lift, too little fuel or a rough flight. Players learn spaceflight the way real engineers do: build, test, learn and improve.

The Game Benefits

Rocket Lab benefits students, young learners and the wider community by:

  • Introducing the fundamentals of rocket engineering and lunar exploration through real physics: gravity, air drag, thrust and orbits.
  • Showing how thrust, mass and fuel decide whether a rocket can lift off and how far it can travel.
  • Teaching mission planning through three lunar missions (crew landing, satellite deployment and rover delivery), each with its own objective.
  • Encouraging problem-solving through six flight challenges based on real launches, such as Max-Q, wind shear and a jammed stage, and through learning from every failed attempt.
  • Introducing resource and budget management through part costs, fuel trade-offs and launch windows that trade safety against reward.
  • Teaching step by step through Flight School, where a Mission Control voice explains the science as players build and fly their first rocket.
  • Inspiring young learners to explore careers in science, technology, engineering and space exploration.

Our Goal

Our goal is to make space exploration accessible and engaging by letting players experience the real engineering decisions behind planning and flying a lunar mission.

Rocket Lab aims to bridge the gap between space science in theory and hands-on learning. Players design, test, launch and improve their own rockets, and learn from each attempt. Through flight challenges based on real launches and mission-based gameplay, we hope to spark curiosity about aerospace engineering and inspire the next generation of space explorers.

The current game covers the full mission journey: guided lessons in Flight School, rocket design, launch preparation, flight through real-world challenges, and lunar payload delivery that builds a lasting network on the Moon.
